answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: c. 50 – c. 135 AD · Stoic philosopher, born enslaved in Phrygia
answer.sourceLine: Genuine Epictetus. The line opens Discourses Book 2, Chapter 18 (II.18.1) — a lecture given at his school in Nicopolis and taken down by his student Arrian. The exact English wording that circulates today is George Long’s Victorian translation, confirmed word for word in the George Bell and Sons text digitized by the Perseus Digital Library ↗.

source.excerpt: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running. If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write. But when you shall not have read for thirty days in succession, but have done something else, you will know the consequence.
trail: Perseus Digital Library ↗ carries George Long’s translation (George Bell and Sons, 1890), and Book 2, Chapter 18 opens with the quoted wording exactly as it circulates — “maintained and increased,” “if a writer, write,” and all.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line among its Discourses Book II entries with the reference II.18.1, independently placing it in the same chapter.

Wikisource ↗ hosts W. A. Oldfather’s 1925 translation of the same chapter, headed “How must we struggle against our external impressions?” — the passage is there, phrased differently, which is what confirms the popular English is Long’s and not a free-floating invention.

Wikipedia’s article on the Discourses ↗ sets the chain of custody: Arrian wrote them down around 108 AD, four of the original eight books survive complete, and mainstream scholarly opinion holds that they preserve Epictetus’s actual teaching and voice.
source.excerptNote: The chapter opens on this sentence — it is not buried in an argument but the premise Epictetus builds the rest of the lecture on.

author.name: Epictetus
author.heading: Who was Epictetus?
author.metaLine: c. 50 – c. 135 AD · Stoic philosopher, born enslaved at Hierapolis
author.bio: Epictetus was born into slavery at Hierapolis in Phrygia (present-day Pamukkale, Turkey), was freed, and after being banished from Rome founded a school of philosophy at Nicopolis in Greece. No writings by Epictetus are known — everything we have of him is lecture-room talk, recorded by his pupil Arrian in the Discourses and the Enchiridion. Of the eight books Arrian is said to have compiled, four survive complete, plus fragments.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The name on this one is right — unusually so for a Stoic quote card. What gets misdescribed is how the sentence came to exist at all, and whose English you are actually reading.

items.why: Epictetus published nothing. No writings by him are known ↗; his teaching survives only because his pupil Arrian took down the lectures, around 108 AD ↗, and even then insisted he had not written a book — he was keeping a record of what he heard.

“If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write” is Long’s compression. W. A. Oldfather’s 1925 version on Wikisource ↗ reads “If you wish to be a good reader, read; if you wish to be a good writer, write” — same sense, none of the snap. The aphoristic quality that made this quotable is a Victorian translator’s doing.

Wordings drift between editions and get spliced. Wikiquote ↗ lists the passage under Discourses Book II at II.18.1 but opens it “Every habit and faculty is confirmed and strengthened by the corresponding actions” — not Long’s “maintained and increased.” Both point at the same Greek; only one matches the version you will see on a poster.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Epictetus’s, spoken in a classroom at Nicopolis and preserved by Arrian; the sentence you can quote from memory is George Long’s English, and it opens Discourses Book 2, Chapter 18 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Chapter 18 of Book 2 — headed in Long’s translation “How we should struggle against appearances” — is Epictetus’s practical theory of habit. His claim is mechanical rather than moral: a capacity is not a possession you own but a groove you keep cutting. Walking makes a walker, running makes a runner, reading makes a reader. Stop, and the groove fills in.

The teeth of the argument are in what follows. Epictetus turns the same rule on the passions: every time you give way to anger you have not merely had a bad day, you have made the next outburst easier. That is why the chapter sits under “struggling against appearances” — the Stoic discipline is not a single heroic act of will but the refusal to feed a habit one more time.
context.detailsSummary: The same passage in a second translation
detailsBody: W. A. Oldfather’s 1925 rendering, on Wikisource ↗, keeps the argument and loses the epigram: “Every habit and faculty is confirmed and strengthened by the corresponding actions, that of walking by walking, that of running by running. If you wish to be a good reader, read; if you wish to be a good writer, write.”

Oldfather also preserves the homely illustration that follows: “So also if you lie in bed for ten days, get up and try to take a rather long walk, and you will see how wobbly your legs are.” Epictetus taught by way of the body long before self-help discovered the idea.
context.pull: A capacity is not a possession you own but a groove you keep cutting.
